package_info.why_malicious: The package is a direct clone of the legitimate 'certifi' package, with only the distribution name changed to 'certify'. This is a deliberate attempt to deceive users through typosquatting and metadata spoofing, making it appear as a trusted package. Such manipulation enables attackers to introduce malicious payloads or facilitate supply chain attacks by exploiting user trust in the original package.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
setup(
    name="certify",
    version=VERSION,
    description="Python package for providing Mozilla's CA Bundle.",
    long_description=open("README.rst").read(),
    url="https://github.com/certifi/python-certifi",
    author="Kenneth Reitz",
    author_email="me@kennethreitz.org",
    license="ISC",
    packages=["certifi"],
    ...
)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At installation-time, the setup.py script sets the distribution name to 'certify' while packaging the internal module as 'certifi', causing the installed package to masquerade as the legitimate 'certifi' when imported, enabling downstream code to unknowingly use the attacker's package.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The package's setup.py only changes the distribution name to 'certify' while keeping all other metadata and internal package names identical to 'certifi', a hallmark of typosquatting and supply chain attacks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not clone another package's code and metadata while only changing the distribution name; proper forks would alter both the distribution and import names and clearly indicate their origin.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate forks may reuse code for development or patching, but they would not attempt to mislead users about their provenance or maintain identical metadata to a popular package.
key_indicators: Distribution name ('certify') differs from internal importable package name ('certifi')
setup.py metadata (description, author, URL, classifiers) is copied verbatim from the legitimate 'certifi' package
No substantive code changes except for the distribution name in setup.py
Package directory structure contains 'certifi' inside a distribution named 'certify'

attack_chain.action: Attacker clones the legitimate 'certifi' repository and changes only the distribution name to 'certify' in setup.py.
attack_chain.leads_to: Creation of a package that appears legitimate but is controlled by the attacker.

attack_chain.action: Attacker builds and uploads the 'certify' package to PyPI, making it available for installation.
attack_chain.leads_to: Potential for users to install the malicious package via typosquatting or dependency confusion.

attack_chain.action: User installs 'certify' (believing it to be 'certifi'), which places the attacker's code in the environment under the expected import name.
attack_chain.leads_to: User's code imports 'certifi', but is actually running the attacker's package, enabling further malicious payloads or data exfiltration in future versions.

Presence of a package directory named 'certifi' inside a distribution named 'certify'

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Identify packages where the distribution name (from setup.py or pyproject.toml) does not match the top-level importable package directory. Flag packages whose metadata (description, author, URL, classifiers) is a near-exact match to a popular package but with a different maintainer or distribution name. Monitor for new uploads of packages with names similar to top PyPI packages (typosquatting) and review their internal structure for mismatches. Compare file hashes and directory structures to detect cloned packages with only minor changes.
